newsitem.title: UK: FORECAST-BAe's year profits set to climb.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-BAe's year profits set to climb.

text.p: LONDON, Feb 21 (Reuter) British Aerospace is expected to announce a 75 percent rise in profits after exceptionals when it reports 1996 results next Wednesday, boosted by strong defence sales and a rising workload as wingmaker for the Airbus Industrie passenger jet consortium.

Analysts expect profits to have risen to around 417 million pounds before tax for the 12 months to December 31, compared to 234 million pounds in 1995, or 447 before exceptionals against 330 million pounds last time.
The dividend payout for the year is expected to be increased to 15-16 pence from 12.5 pence on earnings per share up 40 percent to around 69 pence from 48.8 pence a year ago.
BAe's Jetstream passenger turboprop aircraft business is continuing to suffer from an overcrowded marketplace for smaller regional aircraft.

But the big costs of overhauling BAe's commercial aircraft operations in the last five years have been tucked away in provisions, allowing the profits being made from defence and Airbus to shine through.

Although Airbus reported last month that its annual turnover fell to $8.8 billion last year from $9.6 billion in 1995 it is believed that BAe was already cranking up wing sales in line with Airbus's plan to increase its output in 1997 by 45 percent to 183 aircraft.
"Without question last year was the bottom of the cycle for the industry as far as deliveries were concerned," said Chris Avery, aerospace and defence analyst at Paribas Capital Markets in London.

"The production work that British Aerospace was doing would be beginning to reflect the big jump in deliveries that will take place this year, despite the fact that Airbus's turnover was down " he said.

BAe declines to report profits from Airbus, concealing the result by lumping BAe Airbus in with its regional passenger aircraft businesses as the Commercial Aerospace division. But Avery predicts the division's overall operating loss was halved to around 60 million pounds for 1996, down from 118 million pounds in 1995.
"Deliveries of wingsets to Airbus must be rising and the benefits of loss-reduction on the regional aircraft business is beginning to show through," he said.

BAe is also likely to play down recent share market fears that its foreign sales income would be hit by the strength of sterling, since most of that strength has been against other European currencies, not against the dollar, the international currency for aircraft sales.

Company officials told Reuters recently that the value of BAe's work for Airbus, which is priced in dollars, is already hedged into 1998, and its huge Al Yamamah arms-for-oil deal with Saudi Arabia is priced in sterling.
Overall the defence business is expected to report higher operating profits for 1996, up from 487 million pounds in 1995 and up six percent to 255 million pounds in the first half of last year.

BAe said with half-year results in September that the defence order book of 9.2 billion pounds would get a further boost in the second half from new contracts valued at over two billion pounds, to renovate Britain's Nimrod maritime patrol aircraft and supply the Royal Air Force with air-launched cruise missiles.

As a result BAe's group earnings are set to go on rising, with market forecasts of around 85 pence a share in 1997 helping to fuel a near 50 percent rise in the share price in the last year, to around 1235-1/2p on Friday.
"The strength of the defence order backlog should continue to underpin increasing turnover and profits for 1997 and probably into 1998 as well," said Avery.

"There are still a couple of years of 20 to 30 percent earnings growth so there is still some justification in the continuing performance of the share price," he said. For his own forecasts Avery has pencilled in 84p of earnings this year and "north of 100 pence" in 1998.
